Trust Trust

Run the checks yourself.

Four of our privacy claims are mechanisms, so you can run them instead of taking our word. Each runs in this tab, on what you type, with the rules and formats Archie uses.

Check one

The record shows a changed line.

Archie logs what decides what your agent can reach: keys saved, services connected or disconnected, people allowed to message an agent or stopped. It is not a transcript, and it stays on your computer. Each line’s fingerprint covers the line before, so the lines form a chain.

A fingerprint is a SHA-256 hash: a number worked out from the line’s exact text. Change one character and it changes completely, and nothing works it back into a line. The five below are real, as is every one you make.

Activity · Archie

Nothing has been changed. Five lines, chain checked, and the last fingerprint is the one this computer left off on.

  1. A key was saved on this computer.
  2. A Google account was connected.
  3. Someone was approved to message an agent.
  4. An outside service was disconnected: Todoist.
  5. Someone’s access to an agent was taken away.

Where this computer left off, kept in the keychain: 6a5f…f1f2 Last fingerprint in the record: 6a5f…f1f2

Change any value above: that line’s fingerprint stops matching the one stored with it, which Archie reports when it opens. Then work the switch. Rewritten fingerprints make the record hang together again, but it still fails to match where this computer left off, which the keychain keeps. Both verdicts are worked out from the real numbers, and the switch decides neither.

The exact line hashed for line 3

{"action":"access.approved","actor":"user","id":"aud_63b8f5029ce7481ab0d2947e15c8a3df","metadata_json":{"display":"Dana","sender_id":"tg_48213907"},"prev_hash":"dad7781de8adfc3c996bee263b53337253b0c776ac525ebdf77aa6b094f37f6c","subject_id":"agent_7a2f5c18d9b34e07a1c6be82d4930f56","subject_type":"agent","ts":1757934118000}

Run this anywhere and get the same answer

printf '%s' '{"action":"access.approved","actor":"user","id":"aud_63b8f5029ce7481ab0d2947e15c8a3df","metadata_json":{"display":"Dana","sender_id":"tg_48213907"},"prev_hash":"dad7781de8adfc3c996bee263b53337253b0c776ac525ebdf77aa6b094f37f6c","subject_id":"agent_7a2f5c18d9b34e07a1c6be82d4930f56","subject_type":"agent","ts":1757934118000}' | shasum -a 256

64b31a1a73f882ece6c5ff886cf3487403b55723b58f680ccb396075b2ba1f3b

Paste that command into Terminal on a Mac, or a Linux shell with sha256sum for shasum -a 256, and your computer prints the same number. We have no way to reach into that. The rule is in crates/archie-domain/src/audit.rs: fields sorted by name, no spaces, and each line’s fingerprint carried inside the next.

Two things this does not do. It shows tampering and cannot stop someone destroying the record: delete the whole record and the keychain note together, and nothing is left to check, which is different from nothing having happened. And we never see your record, so we cannot vouch for it or prove what your agent did.

Check two

We hold phone messages sealed.

Turn on phone access and your computer starts leaving messages for your phone in a mailbox on our servers. Each one is sealed with a key your computer makes and gives to your phone by scanning a code. The key never passes through us, so what we hold is a pile of ciphertext with no way to open it. It is off unless you turn it on, per computer.

What our servers hold

As it sits in the mailbox: c is the sealed message, n a number made fresh for it and never reused, both in base64 (raw bytes written as letters).

{
  "v": 1,
  "n": "NPoK22FejvyxV/gB",
  "c": "Xj6K8l89vl0XHPUBJ0qIKM0dUyqaYcJzNGMZgr1/2qGwCUjJSKD42OXPq1FIzjXJviFxyyIHEFqOnpBwnQPf5Osf39yCzjOUMKsTse30jdrBL8L0omM="
}

What we can see without a key

Three fields stay in the clear, because a rule and a query need them: when it was written, which app version wrote it, and whether it has been picked up.

{
  "status": "pending",
  "updated_at": "2026-09-16T14:02:41.000Z",
  "app_version": "0.3.0",
  "payload": { "v": 1, "n": "NPoK22…", "c": "Xj6K8l89vl…" }
}

Nothing has been sent anywhere: the sealing happens in this tab.

The key here was made in your browser a moment ago and starts waiting for your browser. The sealing is AES-256-GCM with a fresh number for every message. The two functions are in js/proof.js. The same pair is in Rust in crates/archie-core/src/phone.rs and in the Archie Mobile app, and a test in each opens a message this browser code sealed.

What this leaves open. We hold the mailbox, so the three clear fields above let us see that a phone is managing a computer, and roughly when.

The seal cannot protect the phone: whoever holds the phone holds the key, which is what unpairing and rotating the key are for. And anyone at your computer, past its password, has everything, as they always did.

Check three

Every request this page made.

Read from your browser’s own record of this page loading, rather than from a list we keep. Your Network tab shows the same after a reload.

Reading your browser’s record of this page load.

  • otianai.comThis site: the page, its stylesheet, its drawings, this script.the page itself
  • fonts.googleapis.comGoogle Fonts: the stylesheet naming the typeface.1 request
  • fonts.gstatic.comGoogle Fonts: the font files themselves.the font files
  • www.gstatic.comFirebase’s sign-in code, which the account menu in the top bar runs.the sign-in code

The entries that are not ours are Google’s, and they see your address the way any host sees the address of whoever asks it for a file. One serves the typeface; the others are sign-in, for the account menu in the top bar and, if you are signed in, the check on your plan.

GitHub Pages serves this site through Cloudflare, so both see the request for the page itself for the same reason. Cloudflare also adds one small script of its own, which hides email addresses from bots. Nowhere on this site is there an analytics script, a tag manager, a session recorder or an ad pixel. We have never had one.

What this page is allowed to ask for

The rule under that list is a content security policy, written into the page and enforced by your browser rather than by us. Its connect-src line is every place this page may send anything at all.

  • default-src'self'
  • connect-src'self' https://*.googleapis.com https://*.firebasestorage.app https://archie-4f35.onrender.com https://formspree.io

Those four are sign-in and your plan check, add-on pictures, the billing service that answers whether you have a current plan, and the contact page’s form handler. A script that tried to send anything anywhere else would be stopped by your browser before it left. scripts/gen-csp.py writes the policy into every page.

What this does not prove. A page can only show you what a page does. For what Archie does on your computer, use the ten-minute check at the bottom of this page.

Check four

The pairing key rides after the #.

Pairing hands your phone the key by QR code, in the part of the address after the #, which browsers do not send to the server.

The pairing link, with a real key

32 random bytes, a real key’s length, made fresh by your browser when this page loaded: bbYKukrGbq-uRt4tHb3Gg8FprAIAa_o7zrKzHXAIlKQ

https://otianai.com/app/#a1.bbYKukrGbq-uRt4tHb3Gg8FprAIAa_o7zrKzHXAIlKQ.<one-time ticket>

What our server is asked for

The request line and the host. There is nowhere in it for the part after the # to go.

GET /app/ HTTP/1.1
Host: otianai.com

Your browser’s own record of the request it made: press the button above

Press the button and compare what comes back with the key above.

Where this check stops. It shows what your browser recorded, which is not quite the same as what went down the wire. Your Network tab settles that, and a network monitor settles it for the desktop app.

On our side, the Archie code has a test, the_pairing_key_rides_in_the_fragment_never_the_query. It fails the build if the key ever moves into the part of a link that does get sent.

The edge of this page

Four checks are not an audit.

These checks show real hashing, real sealing and your browser’s record of its own requests. None of them shows how Archie behaves on your computer.

To settle that, take a network monitor and about ten minutes: install one, use Archie properly, and compare what it shows with the hostnames we publish. Then, on an AI account of your own, block us at the firewall and watch your agent carry on thinking.

Nobody outside this company has audited any of it.

If one of the four fails in your browser, tell us. Each verdict comes from the real result, so a red line means a browser behaving differently or a mistake of ours.
